question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
He did not stop until it was remarked that he was speaking at length about trivial things.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. rambling.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "speaking at length about trivial things" means talking on and on about unimportant or insignificant matters without a clear focus. The word "rambling" captures exactly this meaning — talking or writing at length in a confused or long-winded way, often about trivial matters. (बेतरतीब ढंग से बहुत देर तक बोलना)
◦ Example: The old man was rambling on about his childhood for over an hour.

• Since the sentence describes someone who talks endlessly and pointlessly, "rambling" is the most appropriate substitute for the underlined phrase.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "twittering" — means to make a series of light chirping sounds (like a bird) or to talk rapidly in a trivial way; it does not carry the sense of speaking "at length", so it does not fit here.

• Option 2: "writing" — simply means to write; it changes the meaning entirely since the original sentence is about speaking, not writing.

• Option 4: "littering" — means to scatter rubbish or scraps untidily; it is unrelated to speaking or talking and does not fit the context at all.

NOTE

• Other words with a similar meaning to "rambling": verbose, garrulous, long-winded, discursive.

• Do not confuse "rambling" (speaking at length aimlessly) with "wandering" (moving about without a fixed course) — though both share the idea of lacking direction.

question:
Select the nearest homonym of the given word.
Accept
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Except.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Accept" and "Except" are homonyms (homophones) — words that are pronounced alike but have different spellings and meanings.

• "Accept" (verb) means to agree to receive or take something that is offered. (स्वीकार करना)
◦ Example: She decided to accept the job offer.

• "Except" (preposition/conjunction) means excluding; other than. (सिवाय)
◦ Example: Everyone was present except Ravi.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Accent" — means a distinctive way of pronouncing words, associated with a particular country, region or social group; it is not a homonym of "Accept".

• Option 2: "Expect" — means to regard something as likely to happen; it is close in spelling to "Except" but not a homonym of "Accept".

• Option 4: "Expert" — means a person with special skill or knowledge; it is unrelated in sound to "Accept".

NOTE

• Other commonly confused homonym pairs asked in SSC exams: Accept/Except, Affect/Effect, Council/Counsel, Stationary/Stationery, Principal/Principle, Bare/Bear, Bread/Bred.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
They usually allege that there is / a delay in procuring stationery / due to the faulty purchase orders.
option_1: due to the faulty purchase orders
option_3: They usually allege that there is
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is "They usually allege that there is / a delay in procuring stationery / due to the faulty purchase orders."

• Checking each segment: "They usually allege that there is" — subject-verb agreement is correct (They + allege); "a delay in procuring stationery" — correct use of the gerund "procuring" after the preposition "in"; "due to the faulty purchase orders" — correct use of "due to" followed by a noun phrase.

• Since the subject-verb agreement, tense, prepositions and word order are all correct throughout the sentence, there is no grammatical error in any segment.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 ("due to the faulty purchase orders") is grammatically correct — "due to" is correctly followed by a noun phrase.

• Option 2 ("a delay in procuring stationery") is grammatically correct — the gerund "procuring" correctly follows the preposition "in".

• Option 3 ("They usually allege that there is") is grammatically correct — "They" (plural) correctly takes "allege", and "there is" correctly introduces the singular noun "a delay".

NOTE

• Remember: "due to" is traditionally used as an adjective phrase (qualifying a noun), while "because of" is used as an adverb phrase (qualifying a verb) — though in modern usage both are often used interchangeably.

• "No error" questions test overall sentence accuracy — always check subject-verb agreement, tense, prepositions, and article usage in every segment before concluding there is an error.

question: Select the correct sentence in active voice from the following options.
option_1: The neighbours have called the police.
option_2: The police are being called by the neighbours.
option_3: The Police said to me, "I will call the neighbours."
option_4: The police have been called by the neighbours.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The neighbours have called the police.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Among the given options, "The neighbours have called the police." is the sentence written in the active voice, where the subject "the neighbours" directly performs the action on the object "the police".

• Rule — Active Voice: In an active sentence, the subject performs the action expressed by the verb, following the structure Subject + Verb + Object.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("The police are being called by the neighbours.") is incorrect because it is written in the passive voice (Present Continuous passive) — the object "the police" has been made the subject, and the doer "the neighbours" appears after "by".

• Option 3 ("The Police said to me, 'I will call the neighbours.'") does not correctly correspond to the intended situation (the police having been informed by the neighbours); it introduces an unrelated speaker and reported statement, so it is not the sentence being tested for active voice here.

• Option 4 ("The police have been called by the neighbours.") is incorrect because it is written in the passive voice (Present Perfect passive) — "have been called" shows the object receiving the action, with "by the neighbours" indicating the agent.

NOTE

• Passive voice is typically formed using a form of "be" + past participle (V3), often followed by "by + agent".

• To convert a passive sentence to active: identify the agent after "by" (make it the subject), change the verb to its active form matching the correct tense, and make the original subject the object.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Connote
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Convey.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Connote" means to imply or suggest an idea or meaning in addition to the explicit or primary meaning; to convey a further sense. (संकेत करना / भाव व्यक्त करना)
◦ Example: The word "home" connotes warmth and security, not just a physical building.

• Among the given options, "Convey" — meaning to communicate or make known an idea, feeling or meaning — is closest to "connote".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Comment" — means to express an opinion or reaction; it does not carry the sense of implying an additional meaning.

• Option 2: "Criticise" — means to express disapproval of someone or something; it is unrelated to the meaning of "connote".

• Option 3: "Care" — means to feel concern or interest; it is unrelated to the meaning of "connote".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "connote" (to imply/suggest an additional meaning) with "denote" (to indicate/refer to the literal meaning) — these two words are frequently tested as opposites of each other in SSC exams.

• Other synonyms of "connote": imply, suggest, signify, indicate.

question:
Select the most appropriate homonym to fill in the blank.
The children enjoyed the _________ very much.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. fair.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a word that fits meaningfully: "The children enjoyed the fair very much." Here "fair" refers to a gathering of stalls, entertainment and amusements for public enjoyment, commonly called a fun-fair or carnival. (मेला)
◦ Example: We rode the Ferris wheel at the village fair.

• "Fair" is a homonym of "fare" (meaning the money charged for a journey, or to get on/progress) — both are pronounced alike but spelled and mean differently.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "feer" — not a standard English word; it does not fit the blank.

• Option 2: "fear" — means a feeling of being afraid; "The children enjoyed the fear very much" does not make sensible meaning in this everyday context.

• Option 3: "fere" — an archaic/obsolete word meaning a companion or mate; it is not a common word and does not fit naturally in the sentence.

NOTE

• Homonym sets frequently tested in SSC exams: fair/fare, feat/feet, cell/sell, sale/sail, mail/male, break/brake.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom or phrase to fill in the blank in the given sentence.
He is rich and famous and expects everyone to _________ on him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. dance attendance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to dance attendance on someone" means to be constantly attentive to someone, especially to please them or seek their favour, typically because that person is rich, powerful or important. (किसी को खुश करने के लिए हर समय उसकी सेवा में लगे रहना)
◦ Example: His assistants had to dance attendance on him all day long.

• Since the sentence describes a rich and famous man who expects everyone to be constantly attentive to him, "dance attendance (on him)" is the perfect fit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tap dance like mad (on him)" — is not a recognised idiom with this meaning; "tap dance" simply refers to a style of dance, and it does not fit the context of seeking favour.

• Option 2: "dead duck (on him)" — "a dead duck" is an idiom meaning a person or plan that has failed or is bound to fail; it does not fit grammatically or in meaning here.

• Option 3: "give a song and dance (on him)" — the idiom "to give a song and dance about something" means to make a long, exaggerated fuss or explanation about something; it does not fit the structure "expects everyone to ___ on him".

NOTE

• Other idioms with "dance": "lead someone a merry dance" (to cause someone trouble by behaving unpredictably), "dance to someone's tune" (to do exactly what someone tells you to do).

question:
Select the word that is INCORRECTLY spelt in the given sentence.
Traditional people are used to using a calender for their routine activities in rural households.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Calender.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Calendar" — a chart or system showing the days, weeks and months of a year. The word printed in the sentence, "Calender", is spelt incorrectly.

• Spelling key: CALEND + AR (not "-er"). The word ends in "-ar", unlike many English words that end in "-er".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Traditional" — correctly spelt.

• Option 2: "Households" — correctly spelt.

• Option 4: "Activities" — correctly spelt.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "calendar" (a chart of days/months) with "calender" (a machine used to smooth and glaze paper/cloth) — both are real words but with entirely different meanings, and "calendar" is what is required in everyday contexts.

• Other commonly misspelt "-ar" ending words in SSC exams: grammar, similar, particular, popular, regular.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Outer protective layer of a tree.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Bark.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Bark" means the tough outer protective covering of the trunk, branches and roots of a tree. (पेड़ की छाल)
◦ Example: The bark of the cinnamon tree is used as a spice.

• Since the question asks for the word describing the "outer protective layer of a tree" specifically, "Bark" is the exact one-word substitute.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Shrub" — means a woody plant smaller than a tree, with several stems arising from the ground; it does not mean the outer layer of a tree.

• Option 3: "Rind" — means the tough outer skin/layer of certain fruits (like oranges or melons) or of cheese/bacon; it is not used for trees.

• Option 4: "Peel" — means the skin of a fruit or vegetable (like a banana or potato); it is not used for trees.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes often confused in SSC exams: Rind (skin of fruit/cheese), Peel (skin of fruit/vegetable), Husk (dry outer covering of grain/seed), Shell (hard outer covering of an egg/nut).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The question was raised for discussion before the members during the assembly session.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. came up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "came up (for discussion)" means arose or was raised as a topic for consideration. (चर्चा के लिए सामने आना/उठना)
◦ Example: The issue of pay hikes came up for discussion at the meeting.

• The underlined segment "was raised for discussion" matches exactly this meaning, so "came up" is the correct substitute.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "came off" — means to take place successfully, or to become detached; it does not mean "was raised for discussion".

• Option 3: "came round" — means to change one's opinion, to visit informally, or to regain consciousness; it does not fit the meaning here.

• Option 4: "came out" — means to be published/released, or to become known; it does not fit the meaning of "was raised for discussion".

NOTE

• Other phrasal verbs with "come" frequently tested in SSC exams: come across (to find by chance), come about (to happen), come along (to make progress), come down with (to become ill with).

question:
The following sentence has been divided into three segments, A, B, C. One of them may contain a grammatical error. Select the segment that contains the error, from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
He is not rich (A) / so he cannot afford (B) / to buy a expensive car (C).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. C.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is "He is not rich (A) / so he cannot afford (B) / to buy a expensive car (C)."

• The error lies in segment C — "to buy a expensive car". The word "expensive" begins with a vowel sound (the short "e" sound), so it must be preceded by the article "an", not "a".

• Rule — Articles: Use "an" before words beginning with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u sound), and "a" before words beginning with a consonant sound.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "A" — "He is not rich" is grammatically correct with no error.

• Option 3: "No error" — incorrect, since segment C does contain an article error.

• Option 4: "B" — "so he cannot afford" is grammatically correct with no error.

NOTE

• The correct sentence should read: "He is not rich, so he cannot afford to buy an expensive car."

• Remember, article choice depends on the sound, not the letter: e.g., "an hour" (silent h), but "a university" (sounds like "yoo-").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Treading on thin ice
option_2: To be in a dangerous risky position
option_3: Skating on ice fallen in a hailstorm
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To be in a dangerous risky position.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "treading on thin ice" means to be in a risky or precarious situation; to act carefully because a wrong move could cause serious trouble. (खतरनाक स्थिति में होना)
◦ Example: By criticising the boss openly, he was treading on thin ice.

• The idiom comes from the literal image of walking on a frozen pond where the ice is thin and could break at any moment, causing the person to fall through — hence, a metaphor for taking a risk.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Playing with a sharp icicle" — is not a recognised idiom or meaning associated with "treading on thin ice".

• Option 3: "Skating on ice fallen in a hailstorm" — is a fabricated, non-idiomatic description with no established meaning.

• Option 4: "Making a thin ice sculpture" — refers to a literal craft activity, not the figurative meaning of risk or danger.

NOTE

• Other idioms of risk/danger often asked in SSC exams: "skating on thin ice" (same meaning as "treading on thin ice"), "play with fire" (to take a dangerous risk), "live on the edge" (to live dangerously), "a close shave" (a narrow escape from danger).

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. The other half had been sued at least twice, and Levinson found that just on the basis of those conversations, she could find clear differences between the two groups.
B. Recently the medical researcher Wendy Levinson recorded hundreds of conversations between a group of physicians and their patients.
C. The surgeons who had never been sued spent more than three minutes longer with each patient than those who had been sued did.
D. Roughly half of the doctors had never been sued.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. BDAC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence B introduces the topic: "Recently the medical researcher Wendy Levinson recorded hundreds of conversations between a group of physicians and their patients" — this must come first as it sets the context.

• Sentence D logically follows, narrowing to a specific finding: "Roughly half of the doctors had never been sued."

• Sentence A continues the comparison: "The other half had been sued at least twice, and Levinson found that... she could find clear differences between the two groups" — this naturally follows D, as it discusses the "other half" right after D introduces "roughly half".

• Sentence C concludes by specifying what that difference was: "The surgeons who had never been sued spent more than three minutes longer with each patient than those who had been sued did" — this elaborates on the "clear differences" mentioned in A.

• Rule for paragraph formation: Identify the sentence that introduces the topic/subject (usually placed first), then arrange the remaining sentences in a logical cause-effect or chronological sequence, using pronoun/reference clues (e.g., "the other half", "these accidents", "those") to link consecutive sentences.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (BDAC).

Additional Information

• Option 2 (CABD) is incorrect because it begins with C, which discusses a specific detail ("surgeons... spent more time") before the topic (Levinson's study) has even been introduced.

• Option 3 (ABCD) is incorrect because it begins with A ("The other half..."), which cannot logically be the first sentence since it refers back to a "half" that has not yet been mentioned.

• Option 4 (BCAD) is incorrect because it places C (a specific supporting detail) immediately after B, before D introduces the "half of the doctors" that A and C later refer to.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always look for the sentence with a proper noun or general introduction (here, "Wendy Levinson... recorded hundreds of conversations") to identify the starting sentence, and track linking words like "the other half", "these", "those" to find the correct sequence.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
A wide-ranging effort is being made to safeguard lives and livelihoods by addressing the devastating near-term socio-economic, humanitarian, and human rights aspects of the crisis with attention to those hit the hardest.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. destructive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Devastating" means highly destructive or damaging; causing great destruction. (विनाशकारी)
◦ Example: The earthquake had a devastating effect on the city's infrastructure.

• Among the given options, "destructive" — meaning causing great and irreparable damage or harm — is closest in meaning to "devastating".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "flourishing" — means growing or developing successfully; it is nearly opposite in meaning to "devastating".

• Option 3: "emerging" — means newly coming into existence or prominence; it does not convey destruction.

• Option 4: "fortunate" — means having good luck; it is opposite in meaning to "devastating".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "devastating": catastrophic, ruinous, calamitous, disastrous.

• Antonyms of "devastating": beneficial, constructive, favourable.

question:
Select the correct spelling for the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
Education plays a crucal role in breaking the cycle of poverty and child labour.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. crucial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "crucial" — meaning of great importance or significance; decisive. The word printed in the sentence, "crucal", is misspelt (missing the "i").

• Spelling key: CRU + CIAL. Note the "ci" combination before "al", pronounced as "sh" — a common pattern in words like "special", "official", "social".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "proverty" — is itself an incorrect spelling of "poverty"; the sentence already correctly spells "poverty", so this is not the word being tested.

• Option 3: "braking" — means slowing/stopping (as of a vehicle); it is an unrelated word and the sentence uses "breaking" (in "breaking the cycle") correctly, so this is not the word being tested.

• Option 4: "edukation" — is an incorrect spelling; the correct spelling, "education", is already used correctly at the start of the given sentence.

NOTE

• Other commonly misspelt "-cial/-tial" ending words in SSC exams: special, official, social, essential, potential, residential.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. In a study sponsored by World Health Organisation and carried out by Harvard School of Public Health, the global burden and injury indicated that stress diseases and accidents are going to be the killers in 2020.
B. Road traffic accidents are going to be the third largest killers.
C. These accidents are also an indicator of psycho-social stress in a fast-moving society.
D. The heart disease and depression - both stress diseases - are going to rank first and second in 2020.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. ADBC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sentence A introduces the topic: "In a study sponsored by World Health Organisation and carried out by Harvard School of Public Health, the global burden and injury indicated that stress diseases and accidents are going to be the killers in 2020" — this must come first as it sets up the study and its finding.

• Sentence D follows logically, specifying the top two killers: "The heart disease and depression - both stress diseases - are going to rank first and second in 2020."

• Sentence B continues the ranking: "Road traffic accidents are going to be the third largest killers" — naturally following D's "first and second" with "third".

• Sentence C concludes with a comment on the accidents just mentioned: "These accidents are also an indicator of psycho-social stress in a fast-moving society" — the word "these accidents" clearly refers back to the "road traffic accidents" in B.

• Rule for paragraph formation: Identify the topic-introducing sentence first, then use ranking/sequencing clues ("first and second", "third") and reference words ("these accidents") to establish the logical order.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 (ADBC).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BCDA) is incorrect because it begins with B (a specific ranking detail) before the topic (the WHO/Harvard study) has been introduced.

• Option 2 (CBAD) is incorrect because it begins with C, whose "these accidents" has no prior reference at the start of the paragraph.

• Option 3 (DACB) is incorrect because it begins with D (ranking of heart disease and depression) before A has introduced the overall study and its finding.

NOTE

• Watch for numerical/ranking sequence clues like "first and second" followed by "third" — these almost always indicate the correct order of sentences in a para-jumble.

question:
Select the synonym of the word 'reproduce' from the sentence.
Many scientific researches have proved that DNA replicates itself in the human body and is an enzyme based catalyst reaction.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Replicates.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Reproduce" means to produce a copy of; to make or generate again. (पुनरुत्पादन करना)
◦ Example: Cells reproduce by dividing into two.

• In the given sentence, "replicates" — meaning to make an exact copy of something; to reproduce or duplicate — is used to describe how DNA copies itself, making it the correct synonym of "reproduce" in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Reaction" — means a response to a stimulus or situation; it does not mean "reproduce".

• Option 3: "Proved" — means demonstrated to be true; it does not mean "reproduce".

• Option 4: "Researches" — refers to systematic investigations/studies; it does not mean "reproduce".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "reproduce": duplicate, copy, replicate, multiply, propagate.

• "Replicate" is especially common in scientific/biological contexts referring to DNA, cells, or experiments being repeated.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
A _________ is a female horse.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. mare.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Mare" means a female horse or other equine animal. (घोड़ी)
◦ Example: The mare gave birth to a healthy foal in the spring.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "vixen" — refers to a female fox, not a female horse.

• Option 2: "doe" — refers to a female deer, rabbit or hare, not a female horse.

• Option 4: "rooster" — refers to a male chicken (cock), not a female horse at all.

NOTE

• Common male-female animal name pairs asked in SSC exams: stallion (male horse) - mare (female horse), fox - vixen, buck/stag - doe, cock/rooster - hen, bull - cow, ram - ewe, lion - lioness.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
We compelled the teacher to finish the class sooner.
option_1: The teacher was compelled to finish the class sooner.
option_2: The teacher finished the class compelled by us.
option_3: Finishing the class sooner was what the teacher was compelled to do.
option_4: The teacher compelled us to finish the class sooner.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The teacher was compelled to finish the class sooner.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "We compelled the teacher to finish the class sooner" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense, with the structure Subject + V2 + Object + Infinitive (to + V1).

• Rule — Passive voice of "Verb + Object + to + Infinitive" constructions: the object of the main verb becomes the subject of the passive sentence, followed by was/were + V3 (past participle) + to + V1 (infinitive, unchanged).

• Applying the rule: the object "the teacher" becomes the subject; being singular, the auxiliary is "was"; the verb "compelled" (same form as V2/V3) is used as the past participle; the infinitive "to finish the class sooner" remains unchanged, and the agent "by us" is dropped as it is understood/optional.
◦ Passive: The teacher was compelled to finish the class sooner.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 ("The teacher finished the class compelled by us.") is incorrect because it distorts the meaning and grammatical structure — it wrongly suggests the teacher independently finished the class, with "compelled by us" awkwardly and incorrectly attached.

• Option 3 ("Finishing the class sooner was what the teacher was compelled to do.") is incorrect because it is an unnecessarily complex, non-standard restructuring rather than the standard passive form expected for this transformation.

• Option 4 ("The teacher compelled us to finish the class sooner.") is incorrect because it reverses the subject and object, producing the opposite meaning (that the teacher forced "us" to finish the class, rather than "we" compelling the teacher).

NOTE

• For sentences with the pattern Subject + Verb + Object + to + Infinitive (e.g., compel, force, ask, order, allow, persuade), the passive is formed as Object + be + V3 + to + Infinitive, and the "by + agent" phrase is often dropped when the agent is unimportant or already implied.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
I don't like to work with people who are not flexible.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Rigid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Flexible" means capable of bending easily without breaking; able to adapt or change readily to suit different conditions. (लचीला)

• "Rigid" means unable to bend or be forced out of shape; not able to change or be adapted. (कठोर / अनम्य) — this is the direct opposite of "flexible".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Capable" — means having the ability or capacity to do something; it is not an opposite of "flexible".

• Option 2: "Malleable" — means easily influenced or shaped, which is actually a synonym of "flexible" (in the figurative sense), not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Open-ended" — means having no fixed limit or restriction, which is closer in meaning to "flexible" than opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other antonym options for "flexible" tested in SSC exams: flexible × stiff, inflexible, unbending, unyielding.

• Do not confuse "rigid" (physically/mentally unable to bend) with "strict" (enforcing rules firmly) — though related, they are used in different contexts.

question:
In the following passage some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each number.

The challenge in Madras high court to the Emergency-era shifting of education from state list to concurrent list (1)_________ a futile exercise in turning back the clock. Forty-six years have passed (2)_________ the 42 Constitution Amendment Act. In this period, the education sector has seen far too many changes, and most can't be (3)_________ . For instance, a common national medical test now allows students the ease of appearing for just one examination instead of multiple ones conducted by each state. States still enjoy (4)_________ to operate their own universities, schools and education syllabus. Private sector is also flourishing in education. And the policy tinkering at all levels goes on. UGC is restructuring UG, PG and doctoral programmes. States are trying out clustering of schools, closing down smaller schools. Instruction in English seems to have lost favour at the Centre, even though society is (5)_________ headed in the opposite direction. But the moot point is no one entity can claim complete control. It is a diverse ecosystem. Far more important issues than locating education in the Constitution are at stake.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. is.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "The challenge... to the... shifting of education from state list to concurrent list" — a singular subject (the head noun is "challenge").

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A singular subject takes a singular verb. Since "challenge" is singular and the passage is written in the Simple Present Tense (describing a current situation/opinion), the correct verb is "is".
◦ Sentence: "The challenge... (1) is a futile exercise in turning back the clock."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "have" — is a plural present-tense verb; it does not agree with the singular subject "the challenge".

• Option 2: "were" — is a past-tense verb; the passage is in the present tense throughout, so "were" is inconsistent with the tense.

• Option 3: "had" — is a past-tense verb; it does not fit the present-tense context of the passage.

NOTE

• Always identify the true head noun of a long subject phrase (ignoring the words in between) before deciding singular/plural agreement — here, despite many intervening words, the head noun is "challenge" (singular).

It is a diverse ecosystem. Far more important issues than locating education in the Constitution are at stake.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. since.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Forty-six years have passed (2) the 42 Constitution Amendment Act." The verb "have passed" is in the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — since vs for: "Since" is used with the Present Perfect Tense to indicate a specific point in time or event when an action started (e.g., since 2010, since Monday, since the Amendment), while "for" is used to indicate a duration or period of time (e.g., for two years, for a long time).

• Since "the 42 Constitution Amendment Act" refers to a specific past event/point in time, "since" is the correct connector.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "from" — is used to indicate a starting point in expressions like "from... to...", but is not used with the Present Perfect Tense to mark a point since which time has elapsed.

• Option 2: "for" — is used for a duration/period (e.g., "for forty-six years"), not for a specific point/event such as "the 42 Constitution Amendment Act".

• Option 3: "as" — means "because" or "in the capacity of"; it does not fit the required meaning of "since that event".

NOTE

• Common SSC rule: Present Perfect/Present Perfect Continuous + since + point in time; Present Perfect/Present Perfect Continuous + for + duration.
◦ Example: She has lived here since 2015. / She has lived here for eight years.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. reversed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "In this period, the education sector has seen far too many changes, and most can't be (3) ." The passage goes on to describe numerous changes in education (a common medical entrance test, restructuring of programmes, clustering of schools) that are now settled and permanent.

• "Reversed" means turned back to a previous state; undone. Since the sentence is saying that most of these many changes are now permanent and cannot be undone, "reversed" fits the meaning perfectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "turned" — is vague and does not by itself convey the sense of undoing a change; "turned" alone does not fit naturally in this context.

• Option 2: "backed" — usually means to support or move backward, not to undo a change; it does not fit the meaning here.

• Option 3: "returned" — means to come/go back; it is normally used for people or objects going back to a place, not for abstract changes being undone.

NOTE

• Word choice in cloze passages should always be checked against the overall theme of the paragraph — here, the theme is that changes in education, once made, tend to stay permanent ("can't be reversed").

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. flexibility.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "States still enjoy (4) to operate their own universities, schools and education syllabus." The verb "enjoy" requires a noun as its object.

• "Flexibility" means the quality of being adaptable or variable; freedom to adjust as needed — this noun correctly fits as the object of "enjoy", meaning states still have the freedom/liberty to run their own education systems.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "flexible" — is an adjective, not a noun; it cannot directly follow "enjoy" as its object (grammatically, "enjoy flexible" is incomplete/incorrect).

• Option 3: "suitable" — is an adjective, not a noun; besides being the wrong part of speech, it does not fit the intended meaning of "freedom to operate independently".

• Option 4: "suitability" — is a noun, but it means "the quality of being right/appropriate for a purpose", which does not fit the meaning of having independent freedom to operate one's own institutions.

NOTE

• The verb "enjoy" in the sense of "to have the benefit of" is always followed by a noun or gerund (e.g., "enjoy freedom", "enjoy reading"), never by an adjective — a useful check when choosing between similar adjective/noun option pairs in cloze passages.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. irrevocably.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Instruction in English seems to have lost favour at the Centre, even though society is (5) headed in the opposite direction." Here, the blank modifies the past participle "headed", which functions as part of the verb phrase "is ___ headed" — so the blank must be filled with an adverb.

• "Irrevocably" is an adverb meaning in a way that cannot be changed, reversed or undone. It correctly modifies "headed", conveying that society is moving in the opposite direction in a firm, unchangeable way.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "irrevocable" — is an adjective (meaning "not able to be changed"), not an adverb; grammatically it cannot modify the verb "headed" in the structure "is ___ headed".

• Option 3: "irrelevant" — means "not connected with or relevant to something"; besides being an adjective, its meaning does not fit the context of society moving firmly in a direction.

• Option 4: "suddenly" — is an adverb, but it means "happening quickly and unexpectedly", which does not fit the sense of society being firmly/permanently headed in the opposite direction.

NOTE

• When a blank appears immediately before a past participle used as part of a verb phrase (e.g., "is ___ headed", "was ___ decided"), it almost always needs to be filled with an adverb, not an adjective — a useful grammatical check in cloze passages.
